Introduction - February 2011 











##### **Introduction** 

The base metals complex has performed strongly so far in 2011, building upon the gains seen in 2010. GFMS’ Base Metals Index, which gives equal weight to all the base metals unlike the LME index that is heavily skewed towards aluminium and copper, reached 390.6 on February 7.  This represents a 7.5% increase from the start of the year. 

Our analysis suggests that the underlying fundamentals remain broadly positive for most base metals.  However, a key question, in

terms of pricing, is whether these fundamentals are likely to result in further gains, or whether they have already been priced into current, inflated price levels.  Elsewhere, one cannot ignore the overhang of long speculative positions across all metals and the potential for a correction this poses in the near-term. 

Based on such concerns, as discussed in the metal-specific sections that follow, we have tended to opt for a relatively conservative, albeit still by and large bullish, view in our price forecasts.  Moreover, although we appreciate there has been a broad-based increase in base metal prices, we believe that the fundamentals continue to significantly impact on prices, if mostly on the relative price performance of the different metals.  As such, we expect that nickel prices, in particular, will under-perform the sector over the next twelve months. 

###### **Positive demand-side fundamentals remain in place** 

As we noted in our previous One Year Forecast, the general backdrop of the global economy was positive for base metals prices last year and this seems to have, to-date, continued in the first few weeks of 2011.  Chinese growth exceeded expectations, other developing economies performance remained healthy and, although the mature economies recovery was shaky and riddled with uncertainty, industrial production grew strongly in most of these.  All these factors culminated in a firm recovery in metals consumption. Depleted downstream inventories, in the aftermath of the 

2008/2009 crisis, further boosted growth, as consumers moved to replenish, at least in part, these stockpiles. 

As we discuss in the subsequent section, the latest relevant economic indicators remain generally positive towards industrial metals consumption.  At the same time, given the potential for a slow-down to emerge later in the year and the higher base, it is hard to see demand growth come close to last year’s levels in 2011. 

###### **Investors continue to have a positive impact on prices** 

Investment demand, which was strong throughout last year, has continued to have a positive impact on base metals prices in the first few weeks of 2011.  This continues to be fuelled partly by speculators having bought into the above-discussed fundamental improvements and partly by inflationary expectations given a loose monetary policy environment in most “western” countries and strong growth in the developing world. 

###### **Remember the downside potential** 

While we accept the general backdrop remains broadly positive for base metals prices, we believe that this as well as further improvements going forward have already been reflected in the remarkable price gains seen in the last couple of months.  As such, although we would not altogether rule it out, we find noteworthy increases from current levels increasingly hard to envisage. 

Elsewhere, the increasing reliance of high prices on continued investment demand renders them prone to corrections, were one o

f the numerous potential triggers for liquidations to emerge over the next few weeks. Such could include negative developments in one of the European countries with problematic fiscal balances, news suggesting further, more aggressive, tightening of Chinese monetary policy or worse than expected economic indicators related to the industrial sector. Fixed asset investment rose 24.5% for the whole year of 2010, decelerating marginally from 24.9% over the first 11 months of the year. The overall growth was impressive given the high base seen in the previous year. Looking ahead, further controls over bank lending and real estate investment, as well as a new levy on property in trial cities Shanghai and Chongqing, pose downside risk. Meanwhile, industrial production growth remained at a high level, accelerating from 13.3% in November to 13.5% in December on a year-on-year basis. Having said this, Chinese industrial production had been cooling over 2010 which, given the expected easing of domestic demand growth from the aforementioned high base, is likely to continue over the coming year. In the United States, the January ISM manufacturing index jumped to 60.8, well above its fourth quarter average of 57.3 in 2010. The increase showed the strength of the American manufacturing sector and the accelerating recovery this year. New orders rose by 5.8 points to 67.8 in January, reflecting the positive outlook for production, and was accompanied by an improved employment index which rose by 2.8 points during the same period. In respect of consumer sentiment, the Conference Board index of consumer confidence increased greatly to 60.6 as the year started, which was only the third time the index surpassed 60 since 2008. The growth was mainly led by the expectations component, however, it is worth noting that the January figure was still lower than pre-recession levels, indicating that confidence levels are not high enough to significantly support spending. The US auto industry remained steady. Seasonally adjusted annualized vehicle sales stood at 12.6 million units in January, up slightly from the 12.5 million level that was seen last December and 17% higher than the same period last year. The improvement can be ascribed to the relatively easier access to credit and enhanced labour market, which has strengthened the confidence of many consumers to replace their old vehicles. **A1** Independent - Informed - International Aluminium - February 2011 ###### **Market background** The uptrend in aluminium prices, which saw the cash quote finish 2010 on a 2-year high of $2,461/tonne, has essentially continued in 2011. The monthly average price in January at $2,440/tonne was 3.8% up on December and represented the highest average since September 2008. In early February, the cash quote is around $2,500/tonne, up 2% from the beginning of the year. The improvement in price has come about despite another rise in inventories. So far this year, LME inventories have increased by over 300,000 tonnes and now stand at over 4.6m tonnes. Producer inventories of unwrought metal remain at elevated levels of close to 1.35m tonnes, some 13% higher than the level seen in the summer of 2010. Unfortunately reliable data is not available for stock changes within the huge Chinese market. However, the anecdotal evidence that we r

eceive on this market does not imply a large build of unreported inventories that was, for example, seen in the copper market in the early part of 2010. Indeed, GFMS believe that Chinese stocks have declined in recent months as domestic primary output had fallen. ###### **Supply cutbacks start to be reversed** We have noted the decline in Chinese production, which accounts for approximately 40% of global output. The reduction in production reflected a number of factors, mostly energy rather than price related. The most significant of which was the need to curb power usage by energy-intensive industries with the aluminium smelting sector a key target. These curbs, together with a programme of idling small-scale inefficient capacity, had a significant impact on production levels within the country. From a monthly high of 1.424m tonnes (47,500 tpd) in June, Chinese primary aluminium output fell by 16% to 39,900 tpd in November. Importantly, the December 2010 figure was 1% up from the November low, which raises the question of both the duration and the effectiveness of the production cutbacks in place within China. ###### **~~Aluminium Premiums~~** 200

Meanwhile the Intalco smelter is operating under its current 17-month contract. As a result, their production will be 137,000 tonnes higher in 2011. Later in January, Alcoa announced that it and the China Power Investment Corporation (CPI) will collaborate on a broad range of aluminum and energy projects, including smelters representing more than $7.5 billion of potential investment over the coming years, under a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) signed by the companies. ###### **Producers are upbeat about demand prospects** As we commented in our previous reports, aluminium consumption (along with most other industrial metals) enjoyed a strong rebound in consumption in 2010. Some of the producers appear to be similarly upbeat about the demand prospects for 2011. Rusal, for example, is forecasting 8% demand growth, while Alcoa projects a 12% rise. It is interesting to note that not all companies share the optimism. Some extrusion suppliers are highlighting that offtake from the construction sector remains weak. The latest data on the North American market shows that shipments from service centres fell to a seven-month low in December. Shipments fell by 11.1% month-on-month, however they rose 26.7% year-on-year in the United States and 16.7% higher in Canada. For 2010 as a whole US shipments rose by 25%, while Canadian shipments were 7.7% higher. Suppliers are upbeat about the demand prospects for 2011 in the USA; however views on the European markets are more mixed. We understand that there is little appetite on the part of consumers to commit to deals at current prices given that underlying demand conditions remain weak. Recent data has indicated there has been some moderation in the pace of growth of demand in some regions. Support for our view that many of the largest global economies will not see aluminium consumption return to former peak levels and that European demand is still far from stellar in aggregate came from two major global players in early 2011. Somewhat surprisingly, Japanese shipments of aluminium products in November rose 4.9% to 183,613 tonnes compared to the prior month, helped by f

irm exports and demand from the beverage sector. That said, demand from the automotive sector is falling and with demand from the beverage sector likely to drop for seasonal reasons the outlook is bleak from this region. Therefore, it is in line with expectations that most term premiums for primary aluminium shipments to Japan for the first quarter of 2011 were agreed at $112-$113 per tonne, down from $116 to $118 per tonne in the previous quarter. ###### **Chinese data remains positive** The vast majority of the figures relating to the Chinese market highlight both the strong growth in production and consumption.
